title: Phenological Shifts in the Ruby-Throated Hummingbird and Preferred Flowers

yaml.title: Phenological Shifts in the Ruby-Throated Hummingbird and Preferred Flowers
yaml.author: Aubrey Monaco
yaml.subtitle: GEO511 Final Project

markdown.markdown:
With warming temperatures due to anthropogenic climate change, bird migration times are shifting, and they are tending to migrate back to their breeding grounds earlier each year. Conversely, flowers that certain migrating birds, like Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris), feed on may not be changing the time of their first bloom. Therefore, when birds that rely on flowers as food sources migrate back earlier, they may not have enough food to support them when they arrive. I want to investigate how a pollinating bird species, the Ruby-throated Hummingbird, has been shifting its migration patterns and how the appearances of species it prefers to feed on, the Cardinal Flower (Lobelia cardinalis), the Trumpet Creeper (Campsis radicans), and Scarlet Beebalm (Monarda didyma) has changed (or not changed) over the past 8 years. I predict that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are migrating back earlier each year, and they are arriving at increasing latitudes earlier than lower latitudes. Additionally, I suppose that the first sightings of these flowers in the months that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds migrate back North will be earlier compared to previous years, but not to the same extent as the bird migrations.


# Materials and methods

Narrative: Clear narrative description of the data sources and methods. Includes data from at least two sources that were integrated / merged in R.

Code: The code associated with the project is well organized and easy to follow. Demonstrates mastery of R graphics and functions.

Data: The underlying data are publicly accessible via the web and downloaded/accessed within the Rmd script. If you want to use your own data, you must make it available on a website (e.g. Figshare) so that others are able to re-run your code.

3. I used the Lubridate package to standardize the format all of the dates in my flower data. Then, I used this standardized data to create a year column, where I pulled the years from the dates, and a year_day column, to transform the date into a day out of 365, and a month column to pull the month from the dates.
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
all_flower <- all_flower %>%
  mutate(observed_on = parse_date_time(observed_on, orders = c("mdy", "ydm", "dmy"))) %>%
  mutate(year = year(observed_on)) %>%
  mutate(year_day = yday(observed_on)) %>%
  mutate(month = month(observed_on)) %>%
  mutate(last_yes_year = NULL,
         last_yes_month = NULL,
         last_yes_doy = NULL,
         last_yes_day = NULL,
         last_yes_day = NULL, 
         phenophase_id = NULL,
         phenophase_description = NULL,
         kingdom = NULL,
         genus = NULL,
         elevation_in_meters = NULL,
         state = NULL,
         user_login = NULL,
         user_id = NULL,
         user_name = NULL,
         numdays_since_prior_no = NULL,
         numdays_until_next_no = NULL,
         positional_accuracy = NULL,
         geoprivacy = NULL,
         public_positional_accuracy = NULL,
         positioning_method = NULL,
         positioning_device = NULL,
         updated_at = NULL)
```

4. I found the mean date of first sightings of the selected flowers from 2010 to 2017 and from June to September (when ruby-throats are most abundant) to compare data from the last 8 years to. The mean date of flower sightings was March 10th (the 69th day of the year).
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fl_early <- all_flower %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017) & month %in% c(7, 8, 9))

fl_early_24 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 24 & latitude < 33) %>%
  mutate(mean24 = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) 

fl_early_33 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 33 & latitude < 39) %>%
  mutate(mean30 = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early_39 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 39 & latitude <= 50) %>%
  mutate(mean42 = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) 

flearly1 <- fl_early_24 %>% full_join(fl_early_33)
flearly <- fl_early_39 %>% full_join(flearly1)

flower_early_all <- all_flower %>% full_join(flearly)
```


5. I created the dataset to see trends between 2018 and 2025, and in months Janurary to May. I separated sightings into 5 bands of latitude (in increments of approxiamtely 3, excepting 27 to 33, since there were so few observations). I rejoined all of these bands into one dataset to plot on a map. I also created a difference column, showing the difference in days of arrival between the new dataset and the 2010 to 2014 average using mean - mean1014.
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
flower_new <- flower_early_all %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025) & month %in% c(7, 8, 9)) %>%
  mutate(mean1014 = case_when(latitude >= 24 & latitude < 30 ~ 214.4615
,
                          latitude > 30 & latitude < 33 ~ 214.4615,
                          latitude > 33 & latitude < 36 ~ 221.44,
                          latitude > 36 & latitude < 39 ~ 221.44,
                          latitude > 39 & latitude < 42 ~ 223.3014,
                          latitude > 42 & latitude < 49 ~ 223.3014))

fl_27 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude >= 25 & latitude < 33) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean1014)

fl_33 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 33 & latitude < 36) %>%
  mutate(av = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = av - mean1014)

fl_36 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 36 & latitude < 39) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean1014)

fl_39 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 39 & latitude <= 42) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean1014)

fl_42 <- flower_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 42 & latitude <= 46.64694) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean1014)

fl_1 <- fl_27 %>% full_join(fl_33)
fl_2 <- fl_36 %>% full_join(fl_39)
fl_3 <- fl_42 %>% full_join(fl_2)

fl_4 <- fl_1 %>% full_join(fl_2)

fl_all <- fl_3 %>%
  full_join(fl_4)

```

8. I then created color palettes using viridis scales and colorNumeric from the Leaflet package for my two maps, specifying to use the difference column in each dataset to map the colors to.
```{r}

cpal <- colorNumeric(palette = "mako", domain = fl_all$difference, na.color = NA)

rpal <- colorNumeric(palette = "mako", domain = rubythroat_all$difference, na.color = NA)
 
```


### Trends in Flower Blooms (2018 - 2025)
```{r}
leaflet(fl_all) %>%
  addProviderTiles(provider = "Esri") %>%
  addSimpleGraticule(interval = 3) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(~longitude, ~ latitude, radius = 1, color = ~cpal(difference)) %>%
  addLegend(pal = cpal, values = ~difference, title = "Difference From 2010-2017 Average (days)", position = "bottomleft")
```


### Trends in Ruby-Throated Hummingbird Sightings (2018 - 2025)
```{r}
leaflet(rubythroat_all) %>%
  addProviderTiles(provider = "Esri") %>%
  addSimpleGraticule(interval = 3) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(~Longitude, ~ Latitude, radius = 1, color = ~rpal(difference)) %>%
  addLegend(pal = rpal, values = ~difference, title = "Difference From 2010-2017 Average (days)", position = "bottomleft") 
```


## Download and clean all required data

To download Ruby-throated Hummingbird data from eBird on your own, visit: https://media.ebird.org/catalog?birdOnly=true&taxonCode=rthhum, filter by year (I did this in two separate actions [1995-2021 and 2022-2025] to ensure I could download all of the data), and filter by location (United States)

# Results

\[\~200 words\]

Trends for the preferred flowers have shown that its timing of first observations have changed from the 2010-2014 average, and at most latitudes, when moving higher, there is a pattern of earlier sightings each year. # Introduction

With warming temperatures due to anthropogenic climate change, bird migration times are shifting, and they are tending to migrate back to their breeding grounds earlier each year. Conversely, flowers that certain migrating birds, like Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris), feed on may not be changing the time of their first bloom. Therefore, when birds that rely on flowers as food sources migrate back earlier, they may not have enough food to support them when they arrive. I want to investigate how a pollinating bird species, the Ruby-throated Hummingbird, has been shifting its migration patterns and how the appearances of species it prefers to feed on, the Cardinal Flower (Lobelia cardinalis), the Trumpet Creeper (Campsis radicans), and Scarlet Beebalm (Monarda didyma) has changed (or not changed) over the past 8 years. I predict that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are migrating back earlier each year, and they are arriving at increasing latitudes earlier than lower latitudes. Additionally, I suppose that the first sightings of these flowers in the months that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds migrate back North will be earlier compared to previous years, but not to the same extent as the bird migrations.
